Whether a case is warranted is no longer obvious. #487 set the suite's selection rule, stated in `docs/tests/TS-04-models.md:19`:

> Models are chosen **one tag per code path** — engine (Ollama vs llama.cpp) × architecture × GGUF layout (vision inline or a split projector) × any size-gated branch — using the smallest tag that reaches the path. A new model gets a case only when it reaches a path no case covers yet.

On those four axes qwen3.8 looks identical to `qwen3.6:27b`, which `TC-MODELS-014` already covers: same engine after #491, same `qwen35` arch, same split `qwen3vl_merger` projector, same dense 27B size tier. By the rule as written, qwen3.8 earns no case.

But the two do not take the same path end to end. qwen3.8 resolves a different renderer (`qwen3.8` vs `qwen3.5`) and a different parser (`Qwen35Parser` vs `Qwen3VLParser`), which is the code #491 added and the reason its tool calls parse at all. Renderer and parser are not among the rule's axes.

## Proposed Change

Trace both models from load to first token, and let the trace decide the coverage.

The trace should name, for each of `qwen3.8:27b` and `qwen3.6:27b`, every point where the two diverge or converge: engine selection, arch registration and graph branch, projector handling, tokenizer, renderer resolution, parser resolution, and the sampling path.

Then pick one, with the rule cited:

- **Identical path** — replace `TC-MODELS-014`'s model with qwen3.8, or leave the suite as it is. Two cases on one path is what #487 removed.
- **Divergent path** — either add a case for the divergence, or extend `TC-MODELS-014` to exercise it, whichever the rule supports.
- **The rule is incomplete** — if renderer and parser are a real axis, say so and propose the amendment rather than working around it.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A written trace of both models from load to first token exists, naming each divergence point with the file and line that causes it.

- `docs/tests/TS-04-models.md` — TC-13 and TC-14 are the qwen3.6 entries.
- Both models are pre-pulled on the testbed.

Base directory for this skill: /home/jack/src/agent-workflows/plugins/agent-workflows/skills/open-pr

# Open the change request

Target:  — the issue this change closes, if there is one.

**This makes work reviewable. It does not decide whether the work is good.** That judgment
happened already; re-litigating it here means two passes disagreeing with nobody to settle
it. What this checks is mechanical: is the work committed, is it on a branch that is not the
default, does the body link the issue correctly.

**Evidence work never arrives here.** An act performed leaves no diff to review, and its
issue was closed where the act happened. If there is no branch, this is the wrong unit.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh pr create --title "…" --body "…"` | `glab mr create --title "…" --description "…"` |
| target branch | `-B/--base` | `--target-branch` |
| draft | `-d/--draft` | `--draft` |
| body template | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, via `--template` |
| read it back | `gh pr view <N> --json body,url` | `glab mr view <N>` |

**`-d` means different things.** It is `--draft` on `gh` and `--description` on `glab`.
A command copied between them changes meaning without erroring, which is the worst kind of
difference. Write the long flags.

## 1. Is there anything to push

Four checks, and each has a distinct answer when it fails:

- **Committed?** Uncommitted changes mean the work is not finished being recorded. Stop.
- **On a branch that is not the default?** If the commits are on the default branch, go to
  step 1a before anything else.
- **Anything to push at all?** `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` empty means there
  is nothing here. Stop and say so.
- **A change request already open for this branch?** Then this is a push, not an open. Push
  and say the existing one was updated.

Derive the default branch rather than assuming `main`.

## 1a. When the commits are on the default branch

This happens, and it is repairable. Repair it, but never silently.

**Show exactly what would move**, and move nothing else:

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD

**If anything in that list does not belong to this change, stop.** Carrying somebody else's
commits onto this branch is not a call this unit makes.

**Ask before touching history.** On a no, hand back and do not continue to the push, because
pushing from the default branch is the thing this step exists to prevent. On a yes:

    git switch -c <branch-name>
    git branch -f <default> origin/<default>

The first carries the commits onto the new branch. The second rewinds the local default to
what the remote already has. Nothing is discarded and the working tree is never touched,
which is why no hard reset appears here.

**The branch name needs the issue number.** With no issue there is nothing to name it from,
so this is the one case where a missing issue stops the run rather than degrading it.

## 2. Write the body

The issue line depends on what this change request does to its issue:

| This change request | Write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| finishes the issue | the closure keyword and the number | the issue closes on merge, not by hand |
| is one of several for it | `Part of #N` | the issue outlives this change, so a keyword would close it early |
| has no issue | nothing | and the report says this closes nothing |

**A closure keyword fires from anywhere in the body.** The parser reads the keyword and the
number and nothing around them, so a sentence explaining that this change must *not* close
#N will close it. On the middle case, write `Part of #N` and do not mention keywords at all.

Keep the body to what a reviewer needs: what changed, and what they should test. Where the
project ships a change request template, fill that instead of inventing a shape.

## 3. Open it, then read it back

**Push with tracking.** A branch cut locally has no upstream, so the first push sets one:

    git push -u origin <branch>

Without `-u` the push succeeds and later commands that ask "where does this branch go" have
no answer.

**Then create it**, body from a file rather than inline so the closure line survives quoting:

    gh   pr create --title "<title>" --body-file <file>
    glab mr create --title "<title>" --description "$(cat <file>)"

**Then read back what it actually linked**:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,url
    glab mr view <N>

The link is the part that silently goes wrong, and the cost lands later — an issue that
closes early, or one that never closes at all.

Set whatever label marks *under review* in this project, on the issue rather than the change
request. Where the project declares no such label, say so instead of inventing one.

## 4. Stop

A human reviews and tests. This unit does not merge, does not approve, and does not wait.
Say what is open and what the reviewer should exercise, then stop.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Committed, on a non-default branch, with something to push
    - [ ] Commits moved off the default branch if they were on it, after asking
    - [ ] Body written; issue line matches what this change does to the issue
    - [ ] Pushed and opened
    - [ ] Link read back and confirmed
    - [ ] Issue label moved, or its absence stated
    - [ ] Stopped for a human

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, closes it on merge. Reviewer should exercise the upgrade path.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.
    Want the body?

When the commits had to be moved first, that belongs in the first line rather than the
detail, because it is the part a reviewer would not otherwise know happened:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, after moving three commits off main onto issue-27-parser.
    Main is back to origin; nothing was discarded.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

An update to something already open is not a new opening:

    UPDATED — PR #30 already existed for this branch; pushed two more commits to it.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

Refusing is a verdict too:

    NOT OPENED — the tree has uncommitted changes, so this is not finished being recorded.
    Next: commit them, then run this again.

The body, the commit list and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

# Land the change request

Target:  — the change request to merge.

**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
deleted.** Nothing else about it interests the person who asked. Approvals, protected branch
rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion — all of that is the
repository's route to the outcome, and this unit walks whatever route this repo requires
without asking anyone to know which.

**If the outcome cannot be reached, that is a verdict.** A failure with what blocked it, or
a revise with what must change first. The one thing this must never do is report *merged*
when the code is not in the default branch.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| state | `gh pr view <N> --json mergeStateStatus,headRefOid,headRefName` | `glab mr view <N>` |
| comment | `gh pr comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab mr note <N> -m "…"` |
| merge | `gh pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch` | `glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch` |
| **pin to a SHA** | `--match-head-commit <SHA>` | `--sha <SHA>` |

**The SHA guard is not optional here.** Both platforms can refuse a merge whose head has
moved. A gate that asks about one commit and then merges another has not gated anything, so
pass the confirmed SHA to the merge itself rather than trusting that nothing changed.

## 1. Can it merge

Read the state: conflicts, required checks, required approvals. A change request that cannot
merge does not need a human gate yet — report the blocker and stop, because asking someone
to confirm work that cannot land wastes the one thing this unit spends.

Note the head SHA now. Everything after this is pinned to it.

## 2. The human gate

**Ask outright: has this change been reviewed and tested at `<head SHA>`?**

Three things that do not answer that question, and the reason each is tempting:

- **A green agent pass.** Whatever ran before this was an agent judging its own family of
  work. This gate is a person's judgment on the change as a whole.
- **Being told to run this.** "Merge PR 30" is a request to *reach* this question, never the
  answer to it. Ask, and wait.
- **A confirmation given for a different head.** A person confirmed the diff they were
  shown. If the head has moved since — or moves mid-run — that confirmation does not carry.
  Ask again against the new SHA.

**On no, or on no answer: do not merge.** Stop and report, with the missing confirmation as
the finding. A refused gate owes the reader the same report a merge does.

**On yes, record it before merging**, so the gate leaves a trace someone can find later:

    gh   pr comment <N> --body "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."
    glab mr note    <N> -m     "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."

## 3. Merge

Pass the SHA. Use whatever strategy the project uses, and delete the source branch as part
of the merge rather than afterwards:

    gh   pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch --match-head-commit <SHA>
    glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch --sha <SHA>

**Where the repo requires more than a merge command** — an approval you can request, a check
you can re-run, an auto-merge that lands it when requirements are met — do that. The outcome
is the contract, not the command.

## 4. Establish that it landed

**A command that does not return is not a failure.** It may have succeeded and lost the
connection, timed out while the platform completed it, or genuinely failed. All three look
identical from here, and retrying blind risks acting on a merge that already happened.

**Check the remote, not your working copy:**

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default> -5

The local copy is deliberately stale at this point. Deleting the branch returns you to the
default branch *before* the merge commit has been fetched, so every file the change touched
reads as reverted until the fetch. That intervening state is expected and is not data loss.

**Say which you established.** "Merged, verified at `<sha>` on `origin/<default>`" and
"merge state could not be established" are different reports, and only one of them is a
completion.

## 5. Clean up

**The issue.** Read the body for a closure keyword before assuming it closed:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,closingIssuesReferences
    glab mr view <N>

With a keyword, the merge closed it. Without one, close it by hand and say that is what
happened, because an issue nobody closed reads exactly like an issue nobody finished.

**The labels.** Clear both the pipeline state and any triage state the work carried:

    gh   issue edit <issue> --remove-label <in-progress> --remove-label <triage>
    glab issue update <issue> --unlabel <in-progress> --unlabel <triage>

The triage label is the one nothing upstream removes. Skip this and it strands on closed
work forever, which is how a board fills with things that look actionable and are not.

**The branch and the tree.** The remote branch went with the merge. Remove the local one and
resolve the state step 4 warned about:

    git switch <default>
    git pull
    git branch -d <branch>

`git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch it does not consider merged. That refusal is a
signal worth reading rather than forcing: it means the merge is not visible from here yet,
usually because the pull has not run.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Mergeable — conflicts, checks and approvals read
    - [ ] Head SHA noted; everything after pinned to it
    - [ ] Human asked outright, and answered — not inferred, not assumed
    - [ ] Confirmation recorded on the change request before merging
    - [ ] Merged with the SHA passed to the merge itself
    - [ ] Landing established against the remote default branch
    - [ ] Issue closed, labels cleared, branch gone, back on the default

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    MERGED — PR #30 at a1b2c3d, verified on origin/main. #27 closed, labels cleared,
    branch gone.
    Next: nothing. This has shipped.
    Want the trace?

A refused gate is a verdict and reads the same way:

    NOT MERGED — nobody has confirmed review and test at a1b2c3d.
    Next: someone reviews and tests it, then run this again.

So is an outcome that could not be reached:

    BLOCKED — two required checks are failing, so this cannot land as it stands.
    Next: fix the checks, then run this again.

    UNKNOWN — the merge command did not return and origin/main does not show the commit.
    Next: re-check origin before retrying; a blind retry may act on a merge that landed.

The trace, the checks and the confirmation are prepared and held until asked.

Workaround for 31b model:

2. Extract the Modelfile: `# ollama show --modelfile hf.co/google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf`

4. Comment or delete the line accordingly. Save the Modelfile
5. Create a new model from it: `# ollama create gemma4-k80:31b -f Modelfile`
Now it will load and run without errors (text only)

content.text:
Diagnosed, and it's the same class as qwen3.8 with a different ending.

**What breaks:** `gemma4:26b` ships a split projector, so `llm/server.go:163` sends it to the vendored llama.cpp — my qwen35 exception doesn't cover gemma4. That llama.cpp port knows an older gemma4 layout: it builds 418 tensors for a file that has 658. The missing 240 are exactly 8 per layer × 30 layers — `ffn_gate_up_exps`, `ffn_down_exps.scale`, `ffn_gate_inp.scale`, `layer_output_scale`, `post_ffw_norm_1`, `post_ffw_norm_2`, `pre_ffw_norm_2` and the fused gate/up.

**Why that's promising:** the fork's **Go** gemma4 model already knows every one of those (`model/models/gemma4/model_text.go:343,408,413` and the scale fields), and `gemma4` is in `OllamaEngineRequired`. The engine that can load this file never gets the file.

**Why the other tags behave differently:**

| Tag | Layers | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 31b | model only, no projector | works — goes to the Go engine |
| 26b | model + projector + draft | fails — projector routes it to llama.cpp |
| 12b | model + projector | passes in CI, but that's an old copy pulled before republishing; a fresh pull should fail the same way |

The reporter's workaround fits exactly: deleting the mmproj line removes the projector, so it goes to the Go engine and loads text-only.

Two things I can't tell from the registry: whether the Go engine actually loads it end to end, and what its projector type is (mine accepts only `qwen3vl_merger`, so vision would need more than the routing change).

Next step I'd take: pull `gemma4:26b` here and test the routing change locally, which answers both. That's 18 GB onto the NFS store. Go ahead?

happens now*. Everything else is yours to hold until they ask.

Volume is not the cost. **Interpretation burden** is: information arriving faster than
meaning can be extracted from it. A reader handed everything and told nothing does your
judging at their rate.

## The default: two lines and a question

    <VERDICT> — <the one thing that decides it>.
    Next: <one step>.
    <run it, or see the detail?>

Stop there.

    PASS — all five findings closed.
    Next: nothing. Ready for use.
    Want the detail?

    REVISE — 7 findings, 2 of them break checks that were reported working.
    Next: fix all 7 in one pass.
    Run it, or see the findings?

    IN FLIGHT — 6 of 9 scenarios clear, 3 failing on one cause.
    Next: fix the shared cause and re-run, ~20 min.
    Want the failing three?

That is the whole report. Not a summary of one.

### The offer is the last line

**If the message contains an offer, nothing follows it.** Not a paragraph of context, not
the findings the offer was for, not one more useful thing. The question mark ends the
message.

This is stated as a rule about the *shape of the message* rather than about withholding,
because that is the version anyone can check. Look at the text: is there anything after the
offer? Withholding is invisible — a message where you held something back and one where you
forgot to are identical up to the question and only diverge after it, so "did I withhold"
cannot be answered by reading what you wrote.

**Asking and then answering is worse than not asking.** It presents a choice and takes it
away in the same breath, and it costs the reader the exact attention the two-line shape was
built to save. A report that just dumps everything is at least honest about what it is.

    ✗  DONE — the parser is fixed.                ✓  DONE — the parser is fixed.
       Next: open the change request.                Next: open the change request.
       Want the detail?                              Want the detail?
                                                  ─── end of message ───
       The fix was in the lookahead, which
       had been…  ← the offer is now a
                    decoration

## What is withheld

Findings · Checked · Risks · Decisions · Not done · Unresolved · Trace.

All of it real, and all of it done — a reader who trusts the verdict never spends a second
on it, which is the point rather than a reason to skip the work behind it.

## The one exception

**A next step that is blocked or failed brings its blocker with it**, because the reader
cannot act without it:

    BLOCKED — staging credentials missing.
    Next: you send them, or I stub the integration and we lose real-path coverage.

    FAILED — migration rolled back at step 4 of 7.
    Next: I need a call on retry-with-fix or revert to the old schema.

**These take no question line.** The choice is already inside Next, and asking again
after it is the offered extra this format exists to kill.

Nothing else surfaces uninvited. A risk that does not block the next step waits until
asked.

## When the verdict covers more than one thing

**One subject, however many findings inside it, is one verdict and never a table.** An
issue fixed across five files with three findings on the way is one thing:

    PASS — #42 fixed, tests green.
    Next: open the PR.

Aggregate only when you judged N independent subjects that each deserve their own verdict —
ten skills, a folder of docs. The test: **could the reader act on one without the others?**
Ten skills, yes; one issue's five files, no.

When they are independent and there are only a few — up to about three — give **one
verdict line each and one Next**. Verdicts are cheap to scan; a count the reader has to
expand is not:

    PASS — reporting-outcomes: aggregation rule added.
    PASS — reviewing-artifacts: CUT-sorts-first added.
    Next: commit both.

Past a handful the list of verdicts becomes its own wall, so line one reports the set:

    REVISE — 3 of 10 need work; 1 is a CUT candidate.
    Next: fix the 3, starting with the CUT — deleting a file voids its other findings.
    See the per-item table?

The worst verdict sets the grade, and the line names **every** count — `REVISE` alone
hides the CUT, `3 of 10` alone hides what kind of trouble. When the table is asked for it
lists **every** item, clean ones included:

    | Item | Verdict | Findings |

A table of only the failures cannot be told from one that ran out of budget partway. And it
is still exactly one next step — ranking N items is the writer's job, not the reader's.

## Verdicts and states

**A verdict judges; a state describes.** Most work is graded, and some is better described —
*half done* and *more than one task* are real outcomes no grade carries. Either way the
first word must come from a **declared, fixed set**, never improvised per report, because
that is what lets it grade before the sentence is parsed.

Judging:

`PASS` · `REVISE` · `BLOCKED` · `FAILED` · `IN FLIGHT`

Describing: whatever set the unit declares, defined where it declares them.

Unfinished work still gets a first word; it changes what the line answers, not whether
there is one. **Progress is not a verdict** — "working through the scenarios" is a status,
"six of nine clear, three failing on one cause" is a report.

## When they ask

**Answer the question they asked, and only that one.** Each question has one home:

| They ask | Give | Not |
|---|---|---|
| "what's wrong" / "the findings" | the findings | plus checked, plus trace |
| "why" / "why that way" | the reasoning, attached to what it justifies | a standalone rationale section |
| "what did you check" / "how do you know" | the commands run and what they printed | a restated verdict |
| "is it risky" / "what could bite" | the risks, each with what would resolve it | risks without an ask |
| "where" / "which files" | the trace | a narrative of getting there |
| "show me everything" | all of it, in the order above | — |

**The 30-second cap applies to the detail too.** It is not the place the held-back report
finally lands — a second wall of text costs more than the first, because the reader paid a
question to get it. If the honest answer does not fit, say what it is and offer the rest:
*"12 findings, the 3 that block are below — the other 9 are cosmetic, want them?"*

Severity order, tightest useful shape. A table where the rows are peers:

    | # | Sev | Location | What's wrong | Smallest fix |

**On a PASS, `Checked` is the whole substance** — no findings justify the verdict, so what
was actually run is all that makes it worth anything. Name the command and its result.
Asserting "verified" without the observation is the costliest slop there is; every later
decision rests on it.

**Then stop.** Do not re-offer the remaining sections, do not summarise what was just
given, and do not close with a next step that was already stated. The answer ends when the
question is answered.

## Diagrams

ASCII only, only in the detail, only when the thing has a **shape** — a sequence, a break
in one, a dependency, a before-and-after:

    scrape ──► parse ──► ✗ validate ──► load ──► notify
                          schema drift          (never ran)

One per answer at most. Never in the two-line default. Never for two items, a list that is
already a list, or decoration.

## When this does not fire

A skill that fires on everything turns every reply into a form.

- the answer is one fact and the fact is what was asked
- an acknowledgement — "pushed", "done", "it's at X"
- a discussion, a design proposal, or thinking aloud — a report states a conclusion, it
  does not develop one
- nothing was judged; a status carrying no judgment is a status, and that is fine

## The markers

**The buried verdict.** The judgment lands after the narration, so the reader spends the
attention the report existed to save — twice, if it is bad news.

**The volunteered extra.** Findings, caveats and trace shown unasked, or a "want me to
also…" bolted onto the answer. Both spend the reader on something they did not raise, and
both tax the two lines that mattered.

**Progress dressed as a verdict.** A status with a grade-shaped sentence around it.

**Silent omission.** Asked for findings and given four of seven, with nothing saying so.

**Confidence not matched to method.** A thing fixed on reading and a thing reproduced then
fixed, stated in the same voice. Only the writer knows; say which.

content.text:
Because the pattern matches the JSON **key**, not the answer.

```yaml
expectPatterns:
  - "response"
```

The reply was `{"model":"gemma4:12b", ... ,"response":"","thinking":"..."}`. The literal string `response` appears in it, so the step passes. `"response":""` — an empty answer — satisfies it exactly as well as a correct one. The reject patterns only catch `CUBLAS_STATUS` and `CUDA error`, and a garbled answer is neither.

Three things follow:

- **It's the whole suite, not this case.** TC-MODELS-014 and the others use the same `"response"` pattern. Any model that loads, returns valid JSON and doesn't print a CUDA error passes, whatever it says. That's what qwen3.6 proved in reverse: it failed only because its *load* failed.
- **The content check was delegated to the judge.** `judge_mode: dual` runs an agent judge for meaningfulness; the pipeline ran `simple`, so nothing looked at the text. In `simple` mode the verdict is "exit code 0, patterns matched, no CUDA errors".
- **Not a rule violation.** #487's rule governs which tags to cover, not how strictly each asserts. So the coverage question in #492 and this strictness question are separate.

A pattern like `"response":"[^"]` would have caught it — it requires at least one character in the value. That's a testcase change, which you've ruled out for me.

- **The answer pattern.** Steps are regex over the raw JSON, so `"response":"[^"]*4` catches `4`, `4\n` and `2 + 2 = 4\n`, and rejects the empty string. That one pattern replaces `"response"` everywhere.

Based on the search results, here's information about Ollama API options for deterministic sampling:

## Temperature and Greedy Sampling

At temperature 0 the model just takes the highest-probability token every time (greedy). Temperature <= 0 means greedy sampling.

## Seed Parameter

Temperature=0 alone does not guarantee full determinism across all backends because floating‑point rounding and non‑deterministic sampling can still cause minor variation without a fixed random seed. Use seed=42 (or any fixed integer) combined with temperature=0 for fully reproducible outputs. Setting a seed makes generation deterministic — the same prompt with the same seed at the same temperature produces the same output every time.

## Top_k Option

Top_k: 0 or -1 means "disabled". The possible keys for the options dictionary include mirostat, mirostat_eta, mirostat_tau, num_ctx, repeat_last_n, repeat_penalty, temperature, seed, stop, num_predict, top_k, top_p, min_p.

## Other Sampling Parameters

Top_p (nucleus sampling, default ~0.9): Consider only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds top_p. At 0.9, the model samples from tokens that together account for 90% of probability mass — filtering out very unlikely tokens while preserving reasonable variation.

Based on the search results, here are the key strategies for making LLM generation output stable and reproducible through sampling parameters:

## Primary Sampling Parameters

The three key sampling parameters that influence output stability are temperature, top-p, and top-k.

**Temperature:**
Lower temperature values concentrate probability mass on the highest-probability tokens, producing more stable and deterministic responses, whereas higher values flatten the distribution and increase the likelihood of less probable tokens, producing more varied and creative responses. Setting temperature=0 reduces variance but doesn't guarantee identical outputs in all stacks.

**Top-p (Nucleus Sampling):**
Top-p, or nucleus sampling, restricts sampling to the smallest set of candidate tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a specified threshold.

**Top-k:**
Top-k restricts sampling to only the top-k highest-probability tokens at each generation step, after which the model normalizes their probability and samples the subsequent token from this constrained set.

## Best Practices for Reproducibility

1. **Avoid overspecifying parameters:** Overspecified Sampling Parameters (OSP) occurs when setting multiple randomness controls at once (like temperature with top_p or top_k), which makes the effective decoding policy hard to reason about and difficult to reproduce across providers. A corrected approach keeps a single primary control (temperature) to avoid unintended interactions and make generation behavior easier to reason about and reproduce.

2. **Use fixed generation parameters:** Reproducibility means: same prompt + same parameters → same output.

3. **Consider greedy decoding:** Using greedy sampling (do_sample: false) can improve reproducibility compared to stochastic sampling.

message.content: explain what is "response":"[^"]*4

content.text:
`"response":"[^"]*4` is a regex run against the raw JSON body the step prints.

| Piece | Means |
|---|---|
| `"response":"` | literal text — the key and the opening quote of its value |
| `[^"]*` | any number of characters that are **not** a double quote, so matching stays inside the value |
| `4` | a literal 4, which must appear before that closing quote |

Read as a sentence: *the response value contains a 4*.

**Accepts:** `"response":"4"`, `"response":"4\n"`, `"response":"2 + 2 = 4\n"` — the `\n` is a backslash and an `n` in the raw JSON, both non-quote characters, so the scan passes over them.

**Rejects:** `"response":""` — nothing between the quotes, so no 4. That's the case that let gemma4:12b, qwen3.5:9b and both qwen3-vl cases pass while answering nothing.

Two limits worth knowing:

- **It only asserts a 4 is present.** `"14 is the answer"` or `"see section 4"` would satisfy it. It's a smoke check, not a grader.
- **A quoted answer would fail it.** If a model replies `The answer is "4"`, the raw JSON is `"response":"The answer is \"4\""`, and `[^"]*` stops at that escaped quote before reaching the 4. Given `temperature:0` and "Answer briefly", that's unlikely here, but it's a real false-negative shape.

The harness treats these as regexes, the same way the existing `[0-9]+ MiB` GPU-memory patterns work.

      if [ "$active" -le 1 ]; then

content.text:
Here's TC-MODELS-004 rewritten to both formulas. Everything model-specific sits in one place, and the four steps — identical across all 19 — get identical wording:

```yaml
intent:
  user_story: |
    Verify qwen3.5:9b answers on K80 compute 3.7 (DeltaNet architecture)

criteria: |
  Verify qwen3.5:9b answers on the K80 and gives its dies back:
  - Answer contains a 4 (api/generate shows "response":"…4…")
  - Weights are resident on the GPU (nvidia-smi shows "<N> MiB")
  - No more dies than the footprint needs (the die check shows "GPU_COUNT_OK")
  - Model unloads (api/generate with keep_alive 0 shows "Model unloaded")
```

What that changes, against the current file:

- **The story becomes one line in the fixed shape** — verb, subject, claim, qualifier. The qualifier carries the only thing that differs between cases: `(DeltaNet architecture)`. "Validate … runs" becomes "Verify … answers", because running isn't what the steps check — answering is.
- **Every criteria bullet gains its probe.** Today's "API returns JSON with a response field containing coherent text" asserts something no step checks; the new bullet says what the pattern actually requires.
- **The prose about GPU arithmetic goes.** "Each K80 GPU has 11441 MiB. If total VRAM fits in (active_gpus - 1) GPUs…" restates the step's own shell script. The step owns the mechanism.
- **Two blocks disappear entirely**: "Prerequisite: Model must be pre-pulled" (true of every case, and not a claim the test makes) and "Acceptable warnings: flash attention…" — a note, and nothing rejects that warning anyway.

Apply this to all 19?

import re, glob, yaml

 'Check GPU count':     'No more dies than the footprint needs (the die check shows "GPU_COUNT_OK")',

 'Warm up (tolerate transient cold-load retry under suite GPU pressure)':
                        'Model loads (the warm-up shows "WARM_OK")',
 'Vision inference':    'Image is described (api/chat shows the shape or its colour)',
 'Audio inference (spoken word)':
                        'Audio is heard (api/chat shows the spoken word or that it repeats)',
}

def model_of(d):
    for s in d['steps']:
        m=re.search(r'"model":"([^"]+)"', s.get('command',''))
        if m: return m.group(1)

for f in sorted(glob.glob('cicd/tests/testcases/models/TC-MODELS-*.yml')):
    src=open(f).read()
    d=yaml.safe_load(src)
    model=model_of(d)
    multi = any(s['name'].startswith(('Vision','Audio')) for s in d['steps'])
    story = f"Verify {model} answers text, image and audio prompts on the K80" if multi \
            else f"Verify {model} answers on the K80"
    lead  = f"Verify {model} answers on the K80 and gives its dies back:"
    bullets = []
    for s in d['steps']:
        b = BULLET.get(s['name'])
        if b and b not in bullets: bullets.append(b)
    crit = lead + "\n" + "\n".join("  - "+b for b in bullets) + "\n"

    # replace intent block
    src = re.sub(r'intent:\n(?:  .*\n|\n(?=  ))*', f"intent:\n  user_story: |\n    {story}\n", src, count=1)
    # replace criteria block (to EOF)
    src = re.sub(r'criteria: \|\n(?:.*\n?)*\Z', "criteria: |\n  " + crit.replace("\n","\n  ").rstrip()+"\n", src, count=1)
    open(f,'w').write(src)

You don't need to tell it how. The judge never runs anything — it's handed each step's `command`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `exitCode` and duration, plus the container logs, and asked whether the criteria are met (`agent-judge.ts:200-235`). The commands already ran; the criteria only say what counts as passing.

What the parenthetical does earn its place for is **pointing each bullet at the step whose output settles it**. With four steps in one payload, "Answer contains a 4" alone would leave the judge to guess which stdout to read; `(api/generate shows …)` names it.

Two adjustments worth making:

1. **`…4…` isn't a literal.** The other three bullets quote exactly what appears — `GPU_COUNT_OK`, `Model unloaded`, `<N> MiB`. This one uses ellipses for a regex that's really `"response":"[^"]*4`. Either quote the pattern or say "a 4 in the response value".
2. **The judge is told to treat `{"error":"..."}` as a failure and to accept reasonable variations in generated text** — so it will catch the empty-answer case that the simple judge waved through, but only in `dual` mode. The pipeline runs `simple`, where the regexes are the whole verdict. That's the argument for the pattern being right, rather than the prose.

# Open the change request

Target: no issue — models suite: assert the answer, pin the sampler, one wording via the two formulas — the issue this change closes, if there is one.

**This makes work reviewable. It does not decide whether the work is good.** That judgment
happened already; re-litigating it here means two passes disagreeing with nobody to settle
it. What this checks is mechanical: is the work committed, is it on a branch that is not the
default, does the body link the issue correctly.

**Evidence work never arrives here.** An act performed leaves no diff to review, and its
issue was closed where the act happened. If there is no branch, this is the wrong unit.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh pr create --title "…" --body "…"` | `glab mr create --title "…" --description "…"` |
| target branch | `-B/--base` | `--target-branch` |
| draft | `-d/--draft` | `--draft` |
| body template | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, via `--template` |
| read it back | `gh pr view <N> --json body,url` | `glab mr view <N>` |

**`-d` means different things.** It is `--draft` on `gh` and `--description` on `glab`.
A command copied between them changes meaning without erroring, which is the worst kind of
difference. Write the long flags.

## 1. Is there anything to push

Four checks, and each has a distinct answer when it fails:

- **Committed?** Uncommitted changes mean the work is not finished being recorded. Stop.
- **On a branch that is not the default?** If the commits are on the default branch, go to
  step 1a before anything else.
- **Anything to push at all?** `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` empty means there
  is nothing here. Stop and say so.
- **A change request already open for this branch?** Then this is a push, not an open. Push
  and say the existing one was updated.

Derive the default branch rather than assuming `main`.

## 1a. When the commits are on the default branch

This happens, and it is repairable. Repair it, but never silently.

**Show exactly what would move**, and move nothing else:

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD

**If anything in that list does not belong to this change, stop.** Carrying somebody else's
commits onto this branch is not a call this unit makes.

**Ask before touching history.** On a no, hand back and do not continue to the push, because
pushing from the default branch is the thing this step exists to prevent. On a yes:

    git switch -c <branch-name>
    git branch -f <default> origin/<default>

The first carries the commits onto the new branch. The second rewinds the local default to
what the remote already has. Nothing is discarded and the working tree is never touched,
which is why no hard reset appears here.

**The branch name needs the issue number.** With no issue there is nothing to name it from,
so this is the one case where a missing issue stops the run rather than degrading it.

## 2. Write the body

The issue line depends on what this change request does to its issue:

| This change request | Write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| finishes the issue | the closure keyword and the number | the issue closes on merge, not by hand |
| is one of several for it | `Part of #N` | the issue outlives this change, so a keyword would close it early |
| has no issue | nothing | and the report says this closes nothing |

**A closure keyword fires from anywhere in the body.** The parser reads the keyword and the
number and nothing around them, so a sentence explaining that this change must *not* close
#N will close it. On the middle case, write `Part of #N` and do not mention keywords at all.

Keep the body to what a reviewer needs: what changed, and what they should test. Where the
project ships a change request template, fill that instead of inventing a shape.

## 3. Open it, then read it back

**Push with tracking.** A branch cut locally has no upstream, so the first push sets one:

    git push -u origin <branch>

Without `-u` the push succeeds and later commands that ask "where does this branch go" have
no answer.

**Then create it**, body from a file rather than inline so the closure line survives quoting:

    gh   pr create --title "<title>" --body-file <file>
    glab mr create --title "<title>" --description "$(cat <file>)"

**Then read back what it actually linked**:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,url
    glab mr view <N>

The link is the part that silently goes wrong, and the cost lands later — an issue that
closes early, or one that never closes at all.

Set whatever label marks *under review* in this project, on the issue rather than the change
request. Where the project declares no such label, say so instead of inventing one.

## 4. Stop

A human reviews and tests. This unit does not merge, does not approve, and does not wait.
Say what is open and what the reviewer should exercise, then stop.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Committed, on a non-default branch, with something to push
    - [ ] Commits moved off the default branch if they were on it, after asking
    - [ ] Body written; issue line matches what this change does to the issue
    - [ ] Pushed and opened
    - [ ] Link read back and confirmed
    - [ ] Issue label moved, or its absence stated
    - [ ] Stopped for a human

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, closes it on merge. Reviewer should exercise the upgrade path.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.
    Want the body?

When the commits had to be moved first, that belongs in the first line rather than the
detail, because it is the part a reviewer would not otherwise know happened:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, after moving three commits off main onto issue-27-parser.
    Main is back to origin; nothing was discarded.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

An update to something already open is not a new opening:

    UPDATED — PR #30 already existed for this branch; pushed two more commits to it.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

Refusing is a verdict too:

    NOT OPENED — the tree has uncommitted changes, so this is not finished being recorded.
    Next: commit them, then run this again.

The body, the commit list and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

were green while five returned nothing: gemma4:12b, qwen3.5:9b, qwen3-vl:2b,

span, and gemma4:12b's thinking was its own prompt echoed back as tokenizer
artifacts — a real defect the suite reported as a pass.

value and rejects the empty string. It accepts "4", "4\n" and "2 + 2 = 4\n".

Sampling is pinned to temperature 0 with a fixed seed. Temperature 0 is greedy
decoding, the seed covers what is left, and no top_p or top_k is set: stacking
several randomness controls makes the decode policy harder to reason about
than a single one. The cost is that a model's own default sampler is no longer
exercised.

think:false is gone from the three cases that pinned it (lfm2.5:8b, ornith:35b,
lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b). It was hiding the same emptiness the new pattern exists
to catch.

The prose follows the two formulas this repo now carries as skills:
user_story is one line, and criteria is a lead plus one bullet per checkable
requirement, each naming the probe that settles it. Per-case commentary goes
with it — pre-pull prerequisites, the flash-attention warning note, MoE
history, and acceptance blocks that restated the criteria. What is left
differs only by model name and by which steps a case actually has.

input.content:
No issue — this came out of reading the last models run, where all 19 cases were green and five had answered nothing.

## What changed

**1. The suite can now fail on a wrong answer**

Every case matched the pattern `"response"` — the JSON *key*. `{"response":""}` contains that string, so an empty answer passed. In run 35483250598 all 19 were green while gemma4:12b, qwen3.5:9b, qwen3-vl:2b and qwen3-vl:30b returned empty, and gemma4:12b's `thinking` was its own prompt echoed back as tokenizer artifacts (`ĊisĠ2+2?ĊAnswerĠbriefly.Ċ`) — a real defect reported as a pass.

The assertion is now `'"response":"[^"]*4'`: a 4 inside the value, before the closing quote. Accepts `4`, `4\n`, `2 + 2 = 4\n`; rejects the empty string.

**2. Sampling is pinned** — `temperature: 0` with a fixed `seed`. Temperature 0 is greedy decoding; the seed covers what's left. No `top_p` or `top_k`: stacking randomness controls makes the decode policy harder to reason about than a single one. The cost is that each model's own default sampler is no longer exercised.

**3. `think:false` is gone** from the three cases that pinned it (lfm2.5:8b, ornith:35b, lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b). It was hiding the same emptiness the new pattern exists to catch.

**4. One wording per case**, following the two formulas this repo carries as skills (`ci-user-story`, `ci-criteria`): `user_story` is one line; `criteria` is a lead plus one bullet per checkable requirement, each naming the probe that settles it. Per-case commentary goes with it — pre-pull prerequisites, the flash-attention note, MoE history, and `acceptance:` blocks that restated the criteria. What's left differs only by model name and by which steps a case has.

`docs/tests/TS-04-models.md` updated to match: all 18 step tables and the shared one.

## Expect this to go red

That's the point. Seven cases are candidates:

- **gemma4:12b, qwen3.5:9b, qwen3-vl:2b, qwen3-vl:30b** — returned empty last run.
- **lfm2.5:8b, ornith:35b, lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b** — pinned `think:false` precisely because their answers land in the thinking span.

Each failure then needs its own reading: a model that spends its budget thinking is not the same as gemma4:12b, whose prompt arrives mangled.

## What to test

- Run the models suite on this branch and compare against run 35483250598 (19/19).
- For each new failure, read `thinking` in the step's stdout: budget exhaustion versus a broken prompt are different findings.

Base directory for this skill: /home/jack/src/agent-workflows/plugins/agent-workflows/skills/land-pr

# Land the change request

Target:  — the change request to merge.

**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
deleted.** Nothing else about it interests the person who asked. Approvals, protected branch
rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion — all of that is the
repository's route to the outcome, and this unit walks whatever route this repo requires
without asking anyone to know which.

**If the outcome cannot be reached, that is a verdict.** A failure with what blocked it, or
a revise with what must change first. The one thing this must never do is report *merged*
when the code is not in the default branch.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| state | `gh pr view <N> --json mergeStateStatus,headRefOid,headRefName` | `glab mr view <N>` |
| comment | `gh pr comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab mr note <N> -m "…"` |
| merge | `gh pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch` | `glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch` |
| **pin to a SHA** | `--match-head-commit <SHA>` | `--sha <SHA>` |

**The SHA guard is not optional here.** Both platforms can refuse a merge whose head has
moved. A gate that asks about one commit and then merges another has not gated anything, so
pass the confirmed SHA to the merge itself rather than trusting that nothing changed.

## 1. Can it merge

Read the state: conflicts, required checks, required approvals. A change request that cannot
merge does not need a human gate yet — report the blocker and stop, because asking someone
to confirm work that cannot land wastes the one thing this unit spends.

Note the head SHA now. Everything after this is pinned to it.

## 2. The human gate

**Ask outright: has this change been reviewed and tested at `<head SHA>`?**

Three things that do not answer that question, and the reason each is tempting:

- **A green agent pass.** Whatever ran before this was an agent judging its own family of
  work. This gate is a person's judgment on the change as a whole.
- **Being told to run this.** "Merge PR 30" is a request to *reach* this question, never the
  answer to it. Ask, and wait.
- **A confirmation given for a different head.** A person confirmed the diff they were
  shown. If the head has moved since — or moves mid-run — that confirmation does not carry.
  Ask again against the new SHA.

**On no, or on no answer: do not merge.** Stop and report, with the missing confirmation as
the finding. A refused gate owes the reader the same report a merge does.

**On yes, record it before merging**, so the gate leaves a trace someone can find later:

    gh   pr comment <N> --body "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."
    glab mr note    <N> -m     "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."

## 3. Merge

Pass the SHA. Use whatever strategy the project uses, and delete the source branch as part
of the merge rather than afterwards:

    gh   pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch --match-head-commit <SHA>
    glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch --sha <SHA>

**Where the repo requires more than a merge command** — an approval you can request, a check
you can re-run, an auto-merge that lands it when requirements are met — do that. The outcome
is the contract, not the command.

## 4. Establish that it landed

**A command that does not return is not a failure.** It may have succeeded and lost the
connection, timed out while the platform completed it, or genuinely failed. All three look
identical from here, and retrying blind risks acting on a merge that already happened.

**Check the remote, not your working copy:**

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default> -5

The local copy is deliberately stale at this point. Deleting the branch returns you to the
default branch *before* the merge commit has been fetched, so every file the change touched
reads as reverted until the fetch. That intervening state is expected and is not data loss.

**Say which you established.** "Merged, verified at `<sha>` on `origin/<default>`" and
"merge state could not be established" are different reports, and only one of them is a
completion.

## 5. Clean up

**The issue.** Read the body for a closure keyword before assuming it closed:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,closingIssuesReferences
    glab mr view <N>

With a keyword, the merge closed it. Without one, close it by hand and say that is what
happened, because an issue nobody closed reads exactly like an issue nobody finished.

**The labels.** Clear both the pipeline state and any triage state the work carried:

    gh   issue edit <issue> --remove-label <in-progress> --remove-label <triage>
    glab issue update <issue> --unlabel <in-progress> --unlabel <triage>

The triage label is the one nothing upstream removes. Skip this and it strands on closed
work forever, which is how a board fills with things that look actionable and are not.

**The branch and the tree.** The remote branch went with the merge. Remove the local one and
resolve the state step 4 warned about:

    git switch <default>
    git pull
    git branch -d <branch>

`git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch it does not consider merged. That refusal is a
signal worth reading rather than forcing: it means the merge is not visible from here yet,
usually because the pull has not run.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Mergeable — conflicts, checks and approvals read
    - [ ] Head SHA noted; everything after pinned to it
    - [ ] Human asked outright, and answered — not inferred, not assumed
    - [ ] Confirmation recorded on the change request before merging
    - [ ] Merged with the SHA passed to the merge itself
    - [ ] Landing established against the remote default branch
    - [ ] Issue closed, labels cleared, branch gone, back on the default

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    MERGED — PR #30 at a1b2c3d, verified on origin/main. #27 closed, labels cleared,
    branch gone.
    Next: nothing. This has shipped.
    Want the trace?

A refused gate is a verdict and reads the same way:

    NOT MERGED — nobody has confirmed review and test at a1b2c3d.
    Next: someone reviews and tests it, then run this again.

So is an outcome that could not be reached:

    BLOCKED — two required checks are failing, so this cannot land as it stands.
    Next: fix the checks, then run this again.

    UNKNOWN — the merge command did not return and origin/main does not show the commit.
    Next: re-check origin before retrying; a blind retry may act on a merge that landed.

The trace, the checks and the confirmation are prepared and held until asked.

content.text:
Two different failures, as expected — and the distinction matters.

**TC-MODELS-011 qwen3-vl:2b — not a defect.** Its thinking is perfectly coherent ("2 plus 2 is definitely 4… the user specifically said answer briefly"), it just ran out of tokens mid-thought: `done_reason: "length"` at `num_predict: 200`. The model is fine; the budget is too small for a 2B model that thinks this much. Raising `num_predict` for that case, the way TC-MODELS-022 already does for deepseek-r1 (400, with a note saying exactly this), would fix it.

**TC-MODELS-016 gemma4:12b — a real defect.** Its thinking is the model trying to interpret its own prompt: `"ĊişĠ2+2?ĠAnswerĠbriefly."` … "The user is using a special character (Ċ)". The prompt reaches the model with byte-level tokenizer artifacts in it, so it never answers. This is the one my #484 branch fixes by routing gemma4 to the Go engine — locally on that branch, 12b answered "4" cleanly.

So the stricter suite did its job on the first run: it caught a genuine bug that was green before, plus one case whose budget needs raising.

Next: restore the #484 work, rebase onto `main`, and run the suite there — it should turn 016 green, leaving 011 as a testcase budget question. Go ahead?

# Open the change request

Target: no issue — models suite: one token budget (400) for every case — the issue this change closes, if there is one.

**This makes work reviewable. It does not decide whether the work is good.** That judgment
happened already; re-litigating it here means two passes disagreeing with nobody to settle
it. What this checks is mechanical: is the work committed, is it on a branch that is not the
default, does the body link the issue correctly.

**Evidence work never arrives here.** An act performed leaves no diff to review, and its
issue was closed where the act happened. If there is no branch, this is the wrong unit.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh pr create --title "…" --body "…"` | `glab mr create --title "…" --description "…"` |
| target branch | `-B/--base` | `--target-branch` |
| draft | `-d/--draft` | `--draft` |
| body template | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, via `--template` |
| read it back | `gh pr view <N> --json body,url` | `glab mr view <N>` |

**`-d` means different things.** It is `--draft` on `gh` and `--description` on `glab`.
A command copied between them changes meaning without erroring, which is the worst kind of
difference. Write the long flags.

## 1. Is there anything to push

Four checks, and each has a distinct answer when it fails:

- **Committed?** Uncommitted changes mean the work is not finished being recorded. Stop.
- **On a branch that is not the default?** If the commits are on the default branch, go to
  step 1a before anything else.
- **Anything to push at all?** `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` empty means there
  is nothing here. Stop and say so.
- **A change request already open for this branch?** Then this is a push, not an open. Push
  and say the existing one was updated.

Derive the default branch rather than assuming `main`.

## 1a. When the commits are on the default branch

This happens, and it is repairable. Repair it, but never silently.

**Show exactly what would move**, and move nothing else:

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD

**If anything in that list does not belong to this change, stop.** Carrying somebody else's
commits onto this branch is not a call this unit makes.

**Ask before touching history.** On a no, hand back and do not continue to the push, because
pushing from the default branch is the thing this step exists to prevent. On a yes:

    git switch -c <branch-name>
    git branch -f <default> origin/<default>

The first carries the commits onto the new branch. The second rewinds the local default to
what the remote already has. Nothing is discarded and the working tree is never touched,
which is why no hard reset appears here.

**The branch name needs the issue number.** With no issue there is nothing to name it from,
so this is the one case where a missing issue stops the run rather than degrading it.

## 2. Write the body

The issue line depends on what this change request does to its issue:

| This change request | Write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| finishes the issue | the closure keyword and the number | the issue closes on merge, not by hand |
| is one of several for it | `Part of #N` | the issue outlives this change, so a keyword would close it early |
| has no issue | nothing | and the report says this closes nothing |

**A closure keyword fires from anywhere in the body.** The parser reads the keyword and the
number and nothing around them, so a sentence explaining that this change must *not* close
#N will close it. On the middle case, write `Part of #N` and do not mention keywords at all.

Keep the body to what a reviewer needs: what changed, and what they should test. Where the
project ships a change request template, fill that instead of inventing a shape.

## 3. Open it, then read it back

**Push with tracking.** A branch cut locally has no upstream, so the first push sets one:

    git push -u origin <branch>

Without `-u` the push succeeds and later commands that ask "where does this branch go" have
no answer.

**Then create it**, body from a file rather than inline so the closure line survives quoting:

    gh   pr create --title "<title>" --body-file <file>
    glab mr create --title "<title>" --description "$(cat <file>)"

**Then read back what it actually linked**:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,url
    glab mr view <N>

The link is the part that silently goes wrong, and the cost lands later — an issue that
closes early, or one that never closes at all.

Set whatever label marks *under review* in this project, on the issue rather than the change
request. Where the project declares no such label, say so instead of inventing one.

## 4. Stop

A human reviews and tests. This unit does not merge, does not approve, and does not wait.
Say what is open and what the reviewer should exercise, then stop.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed

# Land the change request

Target: 495 — the change request to merge.

**Merge means one thing: the code is in the default branch, and the branch is merged and
deleted.** Nothing else about it interests the person who asked. Approvals, protected branch
rules, CI that must go green, a merge train, environment promotion — all of that is the
repository's route to the outcome, and this unit walks whatever route this repo requires
without asking anyone to know which.

**If the outcome cannot be reached, that is a verdict.** A failure with what blocked it, or
a revise with what must change first. The one thing this must never do is report *merged*
when the code is not in the default branch.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| state | `gh pr view <N> --json mergeStateStatus,headRefOid,headRefName` | `glab mr view <N>` |
| comment | `gh pr comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab mr note <N> -m "…"` |
| merge | `gh pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch` | `glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch` |
| **pin to a SHA** | `--match-head-commit <SHA>` | `--sha <SHA>` |

**The SHA guard is not optional here.** Both platforms can refuse a merge whose head has
moved. A gate that asks about one commit and then merges another has not gated anything, so
pass the confirmed SHA to the merge itself rather than trusting that nothing changed.

## 1. Can it merge

Read the state: conflicts, required checks, required approvals. A change request that cannot
merge does not need a human gate yet — report the blocker and stop, because asking someone
to confirm work that cannot land wastes the one thing this unit spends.

Note the head SHA now. Everything after this is pinned to it.

## 2. The human gate

**Ask outright: has this change been reviewed and tested at `<head SHA>`?**

Three things that do not answer that question, and the reason each is tempting:

- **A green agent pass.** Whatever ran before this was an agent judging its own family of
  work. This gate is a person's judgment on the change as a whole.
- **Being told to run this.** "Merge PR 30" is a request to *reach* this question, never the
  answer to it. Ask, and wait.
- **A confirmation given for a different head.** A person confirmed the diff they were
  shown. If the head has moved since — or moves mid-run — that confirmation does not carry.
  Ask again against the new SHA.

**On no, or on no answer: do not merge.** Stop and report, with the missing confirmation as
the finding. A refused gate owes the reader the same report a merge does.

**On yes, record it before merging**, so the gate leaves a trace someone can find later:

    gh   pr comment <N> --body "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."
    glab mr note    <N> -m     "Human review + test confirmed at <SHA>."

## 3. Merge

Pass the SHA. Use whatever strategy the project uses, and delete the source branch as part
of the merge rather than afterwards:

    gh   pr merge <N> --merge --delete-branch --match-head-commit <SHA>
    glab mr merge <N> --remove-source-branch --sha <SHA>

**Where the repo requires more than a merge command** — an approval you can request, a check
you can re-run, an auto-merge that lands it when requirements are met — do that. The outcome
is the contract, not the command.

## 4. Establish that it landed

**A command that does not return is not a failure.** It may have succeeded and lost the
connection, timed out while the platform completed it, or genuinely failed. All three look
identical from here, and retrying blind risks acting on a merge that already happened.

**Check the remote, not your working copy:**

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default> -5

The local copy is deliberately stale at this point. Deleting the branch returns you to the
default branch *before* the merge commit has been fetched, so every file the change touched
reads as reverted until the fetch. That intervening state is expected and is not data loss.

**Say which you established.** "Merged, verified at `<sha>` on `origin/<default>`" and
"merge state could not be established" are different reports, and only one of them is a
completion.

## 5. Clean up

**The issue.** Read the body for a closure keyword before assuming it closed:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,closingIssuesReferences
    glab mr view <N>

With a keyword, the merge closed it. Without one, close it by hand and say that is what
happened, because an issue nobody closed reads exactly like an issue nobody finished.

**The labels.** Clear both the pipeline state and any triage state the work carried:

    gh   issue edit <issue> --remove-label <in-progress> --remove-label <triage>
    glab issue update <issue> --unlabel <in-progress> --unlabel <triage>

The triage label is the one nothing upstream removes. Skip this and it strands on closed
work forever, which is how a board fills with things that look actionable and are not.

**The branch and the tree.** The remote branch went with the merge. Remove the local one and
resolve the state step 4 warned about:

    git switch <default>
    git pull
    git branch -d <branch>

`git branch -d` refuses to delete a branch it does not consider merged. That refusal is a
signal worth reading rather than forcing: it means the merge is not visible from here yet,
usually because the pull has not run.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Mergeable — conflicts, checks and approvals read
    - [ ] Head SHA noted; everything after pinned to it
    - [ ] Human asked outright, and answered — not inferred, not assumed
    - [ ] Confirmation recorded on the change request before merging
    - [ ] Merged with the SHA passed to the merge itself
    - [ ] Landing established against the remote default branch
    - [ ] Issue closed, labels cleared, branch gone, back on the default

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    MERGED — PR #30 at a1b2c3d, verified on origin/main. #27 closed, labels cleared,
    branch gone.
    Next: nothing. This has shipped.
    Want the trace?

A refused gate is a verdict and reads the same way:

    NOT MERGED — nobody has confirmed review and test at a1b2c3d.
    Next: someone reviews and tests it, then run this again.

So is an outcome that could not be reached:

    BLOCKED — two required checks are failing, so this cannot land as it stands.
    Next: fix the checks, then run this again.

    UNKNOWN — the merge command did not return and origin/main does not show the commit.
    Next: re-check origin before retrying; a blind retry may act on a merge that landed.

The trace, the checks and the confirmation are prepared and held until asked.

gemma4uv (12b, unified vision + audio) need no rename table: their v.*, a.*

llama-server compat layer states outright for gemma4v.

content.text:
Both failures are informative, and one is mine.

**gemma4:12b — my fix breaks its vision.** Text is repaired (`"4"`), but the image step now returns `"this model is missing data required for image input"`. The cause is visible in that projector's header: `clip.vision.block_count = 0` and `clip.audio.block_count = 0`. My loader copies those into `gemma4.vision.*`, so the Go model builds zero vision layers. 26b's projector has `block_count = 27`, which is why it works there. So as it stands the change trades 12b's working vision for working text — not acceptable.

Note the suite caught it only because TC-MODELS-016 has a vision step with a real content pattern. The text step would have passed happily.

**qwen3.5:9b — not mine, and probably flaky.** It answered "4"; the die check failed: 7644 MiB on one die plus a 93 MiB sliver on a second, so "fits in 1 GPU but using 2". My change touches only `gemma4`, and this case passed on `main` 40 minutes earlier with the same image. It looks like allocation drift under suite pressure rather than a defect.

Next: find where 12b's real block counts live — probably in the model file's own `gemma4.vision.*` keys, which my merge would already prefer, or derivable from the projector's tensor names. Want me to dig into that?

content.text:
They're different models, not different packaging of the same thing — and the difference is in Google's design, visible in each projector.

| | gemma4:12b | gemma4:26b |
|---|---|---|
| Projector type | `gemma4uv` (unified vision) | `gemma4v` (vision tower) |
| Projector size | 0.18 GB, 11 tensors | 1.19 GB, 356 tensors |
| Vision blocks | **0** — none exist | 27 |
| What it contains | patch embedder, 3 patch norms, position embedding, and a projection into the LM's 3840-wide space; plus an audio projection (`gemma4ua`) | a full 27-block SigLIP-style tower at 1152 wide, 16 heads, then a projection |
| Where image encoding happens | inside the LM's own layers — patches are projected straight into token space | in the tower, before the LM sees anything |
| Model's own tag | `any-to-any` | `image-text-to-text` |
| Text side | dense | MoE, 128 experts |

So 12b is a unified any-to-any model that has no separate vision encoder to speak of, while 26b carries a conventional encoder alongside a MoE text model.

Our two engines then split along that line. The Go gemma4 model implements only the tower shape: `Layers []VisionEncoderLayer` keyed on `blk`, with `std_bias`/`std_scale`. It has nothing for a patch-embedder-only projector, which is why 12b raises `ErrNoVisionModel` there while 26b works. The vendored llama.cpp has both types (`PROJECTOR_TYPE_GEMMA4UV` and `GEMMA4UV`'s sibling), which is why 12b's vision works there — and its text doesn't, for a separate reason.

Routing on the projector type therefore isn't a workaround; it sends each model to the engine that implements its shape.

That obligation is a regression check, and I already have it locally on this build: 12b answers `4` and describes the disc as "a white circle on a black background", both on llama.cpp, unchanged. I didn't need a pipeline run for it, which is the part I got wrong.

    OllamaEngineRequired; the engine that could load the file was the one never
    given it.
    
    Routing on the architecture alone is too coarse, because the two gemma4 tags
    with a projector are different models. gemma4:26b ships gemma4v: a 27-block
    vision tower, which the Go model implements. gemma4:12b ships gemma4uv: no
    tower at all, just a patch embedder projecting into the language model's
    embedding space, which that model encodes itself — the Go model has no path
    for it and raises ErrNoVisionModel. Confirmed by running both: on the Ollama
    engine 26b describes a test image correctly while 12b cannot take images.
    
    So the gate reads the projector's type and sends only gemma4v there. 12b stays
    on llama.cpp, which implements both projector types; its text and vision both
    work there once the token budget is large enough to finish a thinking span.
    The projector loader accepts gemma4v and refuses gemma4uv for the same reason,
    rather than loading a vision tower that isn't there. gemma4v needs no rename

Base directory for this skill: /home/jack/src/agent-workflows/plugins/agent-workflows/skills/open-pr

# Open the change request

Target:  — the issue this change closes, if there is one.

**This makes work reviewable. It does not decide whether the work is good.** That judgment
happened already; re-litigating it here means two passes disagreeing with nobody to settle
it. What this checks is mechanical: is the work committed, is it on a branch that is not the
default, does the body link the issue correctly.

**Evidence work never arrives here.** An act performed leaves no diff to review, and its
issue was closed where the act happened. If there is no branch, this is the wrong unit.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh pr create --title "…" --body "…"` | `glab mr create --title "…" --description "…"` |
| target branch | `-B/--base` | `--target-branch` |
| draft | `-d/--draft` | `--draft` |
| body template | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/`, via `--template` |
| read it back | `gh pr view <N> --json body,url` | `glab mr view <N>` |

**`-d` means different things.** It is `--draft` on `gh` and `--description` on `glab`.
A command copied between them changes meaning without erroring, which is the worst kind of
difference. Write the long flags.

## 1. Is there anything to push

Four checks, and each has a distinct answer when it fails:

- **Committed?** Uncommitted changes mean the work is not finished being recorded. Stop.
- **On a branch that is not the default?** If the commits are on the default branch, go to
  step 1a before anything else.
- **Anything to push at all?** `git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD` empty means there
  is nothing here. Stop and say so.
- **A change request already open for this branch?** Then this is a push, not an open. Push
  and say the existing one was updated.

Derive the default branch rather than assuming `main`.

## 1a. When the commits are on the default branch

This happens, and it is repairable. Repair it, but never silently.

**Show exactly what would move**, and move nothing else:

    git fetch origin
    git log --oneline origin/<default>..HEAD

**If anything in that list does not belong to this change, stop.** Carrying somebody else's
commits onto this branch is not a call this unit makes.

**Ask before touching history.** On a no, hand back and do not continue to the push, because
pushing from the default branch is the thing this step exists to prevent. On a yes:

    git switch -c <branch-name>
    git branch -f <default> origin/<default>

The first carries the commits onto the new branch. The second rewinds the local default to
what the remote already has. Nothing is discarded and the working tree is never touched,
which is why no hard reset appears here.

**The branch name needs the issue number.** With no issue there is nothing to name it from,
so this is the one case where a missing issue stops the run rather than degrading it.

## 2. Write the body

The issue line depends on what this change request does to its issue:

| This change request | Write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| finishes the issue | the closure keyword and the number | the issue closes on merge, not by hand |
| is one of several for it | `Part of #N` | the issue outlives this change, so a keyword would close it early |
| has no issue | nothing | and the report says this closes nothing |

**A closure keyword fires from anywhere in the body.** The parser reads the keyword and the
number and nothing around them, so a sentence explaining that this change must *not* close
#N will close it. On the middle case, write `Part of #N` and do not mention keywords at all.

Keep the body to what a reviewer needs: what changed, and what they should test. Where the
project ships a change request template, fill that instead of inventing a shape.

## 3. Open it, then read it back

**Push with tracking.** A branch cut locally has no upstream, so the first push sets one:

    git push -u origin <branch>

Without `-u` the push succeeds and later commands that ask "where does this branch go" have
no answer.

**Then create it**, body from a file rather than inline so the closure line survives quoting:

    gh   pr create --title "<title>" --body-file <file>
    glab mr create --title "<title>" --description "$(cat <file>)"

**Then read back what it actually linked**:

    gh   pr view <N> --json body,url
    glab mr view <N>

The link is the part that silently goes wrong, and the cost lands later — an issue that
closes early, or one that never closes at all.

Set whatever label marks *under review* in this project, on the issue rather than the change
request. Where the project declares no such label, say so instead of inventing one.

## 4. Stop

A human reviews and tests. This unit does not merge, does not approve, and does not wait.
Say what is open and what the reviewer should exercise, then stop.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Committed, on a non-default branch, with something to push
    - [ ] Commits moved off the default branch if they were on it, after asking
    - [ ] Body written; issue line matches what this change does to the issue
    - [ ] Pushed and opened
    - [ ] Link read back and confirmed
    - [ ] Issue label moved, or its absence stated
    - [ ] Stopped for a human

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, closes it on merge. Reviewer should exercise the upgrade path.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.
    Want the body?

When the commits had to be moved first, that belongs in the first line rather than the
detail, because it is the part a reviewer would not otherwise know happened:

    OPEN — PR #30 for #27, after moving three commits off main onto issue-27-parser.
    Main is back to origin; nothing was discarded.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

An update to something already open is not a new opening:

    UPDATED — PR #30 already existed for this branch; pushed two more commits to it.
    Next: a human reviews and tests.

Refusing is a verdict too:

    NOT OPENED — the tree has uncommitted changes, so this is not finished being recorded.
    Next: commit them, then run this again.

The body, the commit list and the trace are prepared and held until asked.
